name: Citation Graphs Over Time
title: Citation Graphs Over Time
answer: Citation graphs over time are directed networks where nodes are papers and edges are citations, with each edge carrying a publication date or year. The scope covers bibliographic datasets, scholarly search indexes, and research discovery tools that track how ideas spread, merge, or fade across years. For a working researcher, this means seeing not just who cited whom, but when a line of work gained momentum, stalled, or was revived. The field sits within citation mapping and discovery, part of the broader AI researcher toolkit.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Citation graphs over time are directed networks where nodes are papers and edges are citations, with each edge carrying a publication date or year. The scope covers bibliographic datasets, scholarly search indexes, and research discovery tools that track how ideas spread, merge, or fade across years. For a working researcher, this means seeing not just who cited whom, but when a line of work gained momentum, stalled, or was revived. The field sits within citation mapping and discovery, part of the broader AI researcher toolkit.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These graphs usually run on graph databases or columnar stores that can handle very large numbers of edges and time-stamped queries. Common infrastructure includes open citation indexes, DOI registries, and local snapshots of paper metadata, often loaded into graph databases or distributed processing frameworks for traversal and aggregation. Because the site links to original papers rather than a search tool, the underlying data tends to come from publisher APIs, preprint servers, and open bibliographic records. Storage must preserve the original paper identifier so a node can always resolve to the source document.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by extracting citation pairs from reference lists and matching them to unique paper identifiers, then attaching the citing paper's publication date to each edge. Analysts then compute time series of citation counts, co-citation clusters, and forward or backward citation chains over yearly or monthly windows. A common technique is to build a cumulative graph and slice it at different dates to see how the structure changed. No machine learning is required for basic mapping, though clustering and link prediction are sometimes used.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on provenance, because a citation graph is only as good as its source records. Each edge must retain the original paper link, and the site's practice of linking to the original paper rather than a third party search tool supports that. Risks include duplicate records, retracted papers still being cited, and citation bias toward well known venues. Provenance requires keeping the DOI or other persistent identifier with every node and edge, and flagging retractions or corrections when they appear.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Citation graphs over time are moving toward live updating views that show research fronts as they form, rather than static historical maps. Better author disambiguation and preprint citation tracking will make early signals more reliable. There is also growing interest in using these graphs to spot replication gaps or neglected areas where older work is rarely cited but still relevant. The likely direction is a tighter link between the graph and the underlying paper, so a researcher can move from a trend line to the exact claim or method in the original text.
